summary: Updates RFC 5280, the X.509 certificate and CRL profile. It changes which encodings are acceptable for the explicitText field of the user notice policy qualifier, and clarifies how internationalized domain name labels are converted to ASCII, along with other fixes.

eli5.summary: A rulebook for digital ID cards gets a few corrections: which writing styles are allowed in one note field, and how names with special letters are written.

questions: what changed in rfc 5280 for x.509 certificates
how are internationalized domain names handled in certificates
which encodings are allowed for explicittext
how are idn labels converted in certificates
can a ca use ia5string in explicittext
subtitle: Small but important fixes to the X.509 certificate profile: text encodings, internationalized names and trust anchors.

tldr.problem: RFC 5280, the Internet profile for X.509 certificates and CRLs, had rules that no longer matched practice or were unclear, including how explicitText is encoded and how internationalized domain labels are converted to ASCII.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6818 gives replacement text for specific paragraphs of RFC 5280: it changes the allowed explicitText encodings, aligns the IDN conversion rules, clarifies self-signed certificates and trust anchors, and extends the security considerations.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5280 paragraph by paragraph. The most visible change is that IA5String is now forbidden for explicitText, while VisibleString and BMPString are allowed but less preferred.

today: RFC 6818 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2013. It updates RFC 5280, and the metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Update Covers
sections.content:
RFC 6818 updates RFC 5280, the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile. It does not stand alone: each section gives text to add to, or replace in, a named place in RFC 5280.

The introduction lists the changes. It recommends that self-signed certificates used to convey trust anchor data be marked as CA certificates, which is not always current practice. It clarifies how such certificates are used in path validation. It changes the acceptable encodings for the explicitText field, aligns the IDN rules for distinguished names with those for GeneralNames, and expands the security considerations in light of observed attacks.
sections.eli5: This memo is a list of fix-it notes for an older rulebook. Each note says which page to change and what the new words are.

sections.title: Self-Signed Certificates Outside the Scope
sections.content:
A paragraph is added to RFC 5280, Section 3.2. It notes that self-issued certificates, and self-signed certificates issued by entities other than CAs, are outside the specification, consistent with X.509. For example, a web server or client might generate a self-signed certificate to identify itself.

Both those certificates and how a relying party uses them to authenticate asserted identities are outside the scope of RFC 5280.
sections.eli5: If a computer makes its own ID card and signs it itself, the rulebook does not say how to decide whether to trust it. That is left to someone else.

sections.title: Encoding of explicitText
sections.content:
The explicitText field of a user notice policy qualifier holds a textual statement directly in a certificate, up to a maximum of 200 characters. The old rule said CAs SHOULD use UTF8String, MAY use IA5String, and MUST NOT use VisibleString or BMPString.

The replacement text says:

  • Conforming CAs SHOULD use UTF8String.
  • VisibleString or BMPString are acceptable but less preferred.
  • Conforming CAs MUST NOT use IA5String.
  • The string SHOULD NOT include control characters (U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F).
  • With UTF8String or BMPString, character sequences SHOULD be normalized to Unicode normalization form C (NFC).

The introduction says this brings the text in line with existing practice.
sections.eli5: There is a note box on the ID card. The new rule says which kinds of handwriting are allowed in it, and bans one style that was allowed before.

sections.title: Trust Anchors in Path Validation
sections.content:
RFC 5280, Section 6.2, explains that a CA may distribute self-signed certificates to carry trust anchor information. Extensions such as policy constraints or name constraints can then recommend inputs to path validation. The path validation algorithm in Section 6.1 does not assume that trust anchor information comes in self-signed certificates, and it does not specify processing for that extra information.

The update adds that RFC 5914 defines several formats for trust anchor information, including self-signed certificates, and that RFC 5937 shows how such information may be used to initialize path validation inputs. Implementations are free to use any additional information in a trust anchor representation, or to ignore it.
sections.eli5: A trusted starting point can come with extra instructions, like only trusting it for certain topics. Programs may follow those instructions or skip them.

sections.title: Internationalized Domain Names in Distinguished Names
sections.content:
Domain names can be written as distinguished names using domain components, and each domainComponent holds one label as an IA5String. To store a label from an internationalized domain name, an implementation MUST perform the ToASCII conversion from Section 4.1 of RFC 3490.

The update adds that the conversion MUST be done with the UseSTD3ASCIIRules flag set. The label is still a stored string, so the AllowUnassigned flag SHALL NOT be set. The process is the same as step 4 in Section 7.2 of RFC 5280, which aligns the two places where domain names are encoded.
sections.eli5: Names with special letters are turned into plain letters and numbers before they go on the card. Now there is one rule for doing it in both places where names appear.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The update rewrites a paragraph about protecting private keys. It adds that an attacker may issue bogus certificates and CRLs even without a copy of a CA's private key, by misusing the CA's workstation or an RA's workstation, either through unauthorized access or through inappropriate activity by an insider. Bogus certificates could copy the subject names of legitimate ones, including bogus CA certificates, and could even share issuer names and possibly serial numbers with real ones. The introduction says this was prompted by observed attacks.

A new paragraph notes that one-way hash functions are commonly used to generate key identifiers (AKI and SKI), but none of the security properties of such functions are required for that purpose.
sections.eli5: A forger does not need to steal the stamp itself. Sneaking into the stamp office, or help from someone inside, also works. Also, the number on a key label does not need to be secret-proof.

sections.title: Reference Changes
sections.content: The update adds RFC 5914, Trust Anchor Format, to the normative references of RFC 5280, and RFC 5937, Using Trust Anchor Constraints during Certification Path Processing, to the informative references. Both are needed because of the trust anchor change described in Section 4.
sections.eli5: Two new books are added to the reading list because the new notes refer to them.
